title: New Housing Fund Rules: Take What You Can, But Don't Treat It as Savings
dek: The housing provident fund is not a savings account you can withdraw at will; fraudulent withdrawals are prosecuted and you cannot withdraw again for three years. But the new rules put renting at the top of the withdrawal list and remove the rent-to-income ratio cap, so money you should take, you should still take.
why: Three people in different situations (a self-employed person, a young professional, a property owner) each run their own numbers, turning the 20 clause changes in the new rules into concrete decisions. The second half, on flexible-employment contributions and the comparison with the system-inside track, is especially informative.
who: Employees with a provident fund who aren't sure whether to withdraw or leave it; people considering buying a home, converting a commercial loan to a provident fund loan, or contributing as a flexible-employment worker; job seekers trying to judge whether a company is well-run.
skip: The opening chit-chat about the show's origin and the three hosts' positions can be fast-forwarded; start from 13:10, when Zhou Yi's experience of using it begins.

points.h: Six months after auto-withdrawal, I paused it myself
points.body: After Zhou Yi activated Beijing's no-threshold monthly rent withdrawal of 2000 yuan, she found the money slid into another card the moment it arrived, completely decoupled from the mental account for paying rent; when her spending card ran out at month's end, the money was auto-deducted, adding friction to life. After confirming the fund balance earns 1.5% interest, higher than the roughly 0.95% one-year bank deposit rate, she paused the withdrawal the next day. Yu Bai noted this contrasts with the advice three years ago to ‘take everything you can, use everything you can’, and two young colleagues in the department had made the same choice. Lao Qian cautioned that this is indeed low capital efficiency, but most people can't achieve the efficiency they imagine—people just make fake books for themselves.

points.h: The provident fund is not savings; not being able to withdraw is the norm
points.body: Yu Bai walked through an extreme case: a young person loses their job and goes home with no liquid funds, but has tens of thousands in the provident fund. The home is owner-occupied, so it qualifies neither as buying nor as renting; even though the new rules allow withdrawal for renovation or property fees, if the family has no such needs, there is nothing to be done. If you risk fraudulent withdrawal under a fabricated pretext, you must return the full amount and cannot withdraw any provident fund for three years. So both ‘take everything you can’ and ‘treat it as forced savings with a higher rate than a current account’ are valid; it depends on the individual.

points.h: The new rules put renting at the top of the withdrawal list
points.body: This revision adjusts 20 clauses. First, renovating an owner-occupied home and paying its property fees are included as withdrawal purposes for the first time; the fund no longer serves only loan-based home purchases. Second, renting used to require that rent exceed a set proportion of household wage income; this version removes that restriction and places renting first in the withdrawal list. Third, flexible-employment workers are formally included in the system for the first time: self-employed individuals and part-time workers may contribute voluntarily and apply for provident fund loans. In addition, the management center must reply to withdrawal applications within three days and to loan applications within ten days, and nationwide mutual recognition of contribution records is being advanced.

points.h: The share of contributions lent out has fallen from 70% to 30%
points.body: Lao Qian's data: this year, the share of provident fund contributions lent out is as low as just over 30%, while at the peak it was over 70%, falling steadily in just a few years. That is, the theoretically most stable, lowest-rate, highest-quality loan channel is actually used by only just over 30% of people. This directly reflects how low the desire to buy is. Lao Qian also notes the new rules point to housing consumption rather than leverage: renting first, property fees and renovation withdrawable, thresholds greatly lowered—supporting measures as the real estate market shifts from incremental to stock, and echoing aging: the monthly withdrawal ratio turned up in 2023, exactly when the 1960s cohort retired.

points.h: If you want to buy, be careful about withdrawing
points.body: Yu Bai warns: the provident fund loan amount is tied to the account balance; in some cities you can borrow 16 times the balance, in others 20 times, varying by city. Guangzhou also has multiple caps, and the smallest applies: for a first or second owner-occupied home the minimum down payment is 20%, so a 1 million yuan home cannot be loaned more than 800,000; and monthly repayment exceeding 50% of monthly income is also disallowed. So before withdrawing the fund as living expenses, check your city's loan rules. Yu Bai is also cautious about the logic of buying when ‘the rent-to-price ratio is close to the provident fund rate, and only the down payment is missing’: you must also consider depreciation, price swings, and how to withstand risk once a 600,000 down payment is locked up.

points.h: Flexible-employment contributors carry the full amount alone
points.body: The contribution base and rate for flexible-employment workers are calculated the same as for employees, but there is no employer to pay half, so one person bears the full 10% to 24%. The base must be self-declared: below 10,000 no proof is needed; above 10,000 you must log into the individual income tax app and check tax details as documentation, to prevent inflating the base to obtain a higher loan. Zhou Yi calculated: 10,000 at 10% to 24% is 1000 to 2400 yuan, and this money is not counted in individual income tax, but if unused it is a loss. In addition, most pilot cities require 6 to 12 consecutive months of contributions before applying for a provident fund loan, and most do not allow one-time back payments.

points.h: Inside the system, the provident fund is an invisible benefit
points.body: Zhou Yi asked a friend with a public institution job back home, who openly showed a screenshot of the provident fund account: monthly deposits were more than twice hers, and the balance exceeded her savings. The friend lives at home with no rent, so the fund just accumulates as forced savings or future loan capacity, plus a职业年金 on top, and the contribution base includes all bonuses and subsidies. Lao Qian adds: the provident fund is tax-free, while individual pension contributions are capped at 12,000 yuan a year and taxed at 3% on withdrawal, so those inside the system get an extra layer of tax advantage. On the data: in 2025 the national average annual wage for urban non-private units was 129,441 yuan, for private units 71,590 yuan, while working hours run the other way.

points.h: Full provident fund contributions are a lens on a company
points.body: Lao Qian's judgment on ‘is a company that pays the provident fund a better choice’ has not changed at all: a company that pays in full respects its employees and respects the rules, which means it is likely well-run in every respect, not playing cat-and-mouse with policy. He goes further: this points to not making profit maximization the first goal, treating people as people, and the invisible returns show up elsewhere. Zhou Yi calculated: on a wage base of 100, take-home is just over 70, but the boss pays over 130, and everyone in the chain feels wronged. Lao Qian cites Ford's Model T wage increase—letting workers afford a car and have time to use it was not capitalist conscience, but a better utility function.

quotes.text: It arrived, but because your phone gets so many app notifications you don't look carefully—say it reminds you 2000 yuan came in, and it just sits in that card until the end of the month, when my spending card is used up and it gets auto-deducted from that card.
But the fact is people make fake books for themselves, people withdraw on impulse for all sorts of reasons, people are very good at self-deception.
You really can't treat the provident fund as a deposit, because your bank deposit you can withdraw at any time, but the provident fund you cannot.
And it's the highest-quality loan channel, the rate is so low, yet only just over 30% of people took loans—what was the ratio at the peak? Over 70%—in just a few years.
I think a company that pays the provident fund in full shows it respects its employees and respects the rules.

Treating people as people doesn't mean increasing costs; it also means one person's spending, the household sector's spending, becomes the corporate sector's income, and the corporate sector's spending becomes the household sector's wages—these two are a virtuous cycle.
Take everything you can, use everything you can—buying a home, building, renovating, repaying a loan, renting, retirement, leaving the country—all can use it.
